etymology: A worn-down English form of paralysis, through the Old French paralisie, from the Greek paralusis, “a loosing aside, a slackening”; hence the loss of motion or feeling in the body, the limbs unstrung and useless.
biblical_def: The palsy is paralysis — the body slackened and unstrung, the limbs loosed from the will that should command them, so that a man must be carried where he cannot walk. The Gospels are full of such men, for they came to Christ in crowds: “those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them” (Mat 4:24). The great palsy text is the man let down through the roof at Capernaum. Four friends bore him, and finding the door blocked, uncovered the roof and let the bed down before the LORD. “When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee” (Mar 2:5). Mark the order: the pardon first, the cure after. The scribes reasoned that none can forgive sins but God only — and they reasoned rightly, and drew the wrong conclusion, for the One before them was God manifest in flesh. So Christ gave them the visible proof of the invisible act: “But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house” (Mat 9:6). The healing is the receipt for the pardon. A centurion pleaded the same disease for his servant (Mat 8:6), and at Lydda Peter found Aeneas eight years bedfast and said, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole. The palsied man’s deepest need was never his legs.
webster_summary: Paralysis; the loss of motion or feeling in the body or a part of it; the limbs unstrung and useless.
webster_full: PALSY, the loss or diminution of voluntary motion or of sensation, or of both, in the whole body or in a part; paralysis.
A contracted English form of paralysis, through Old French paralisie, from Greek paralusis, “a loosing aside.”
It names the body that will not obey the will — the man who must be borne by others.
The palsied of Syria were brought to Christ in multitudes and He healed them (Mat 4:24).
At Capernaum the cure of a palsy proved Christ’s authority to forgive sins (Mar 2:5–12).
scriptures: Mar 2:5
When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.
Mat 9:6
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house.
Mar 2:11
I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house.
Mat 8:6
And saying, Lord, my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy, grievously tormented.
corruption_summary: An old word for paralysis; the live corruption is the reversal of Christ’s order — a gospel that offers the bed carried away and never the sins forgiven.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern misuse of this history is to keep the miracle and lose the pardon. Whole ministries read Mark 2 as a healing story with a religious preface, and preach a Christ who mends bodies, mends marriages, mends fortunes — and whose word about sin is an embarrassment to be hurried past. That is exactly backwards. Christ spoke the pardon first and the cure second, and He said plainly why: the visible healing was given that ye may know the invisible authority. Strip out the forgiveness and the miracle has no point left; it becomes a wonder without a doctrine, a kindness without a Saviour. The health-and-wealth preachers who promise the bed carried away to every believer of sufficient faith have taken the sign and thrown away the thing signified, and they leave their hearers still palsied in the only place that damns.

Recover the order Christ set. Man’s deepest disability is not in his limbs but in his will, which is loosed from God and cannot rise; total depravity means the sinner is not merely weak but bedfast, unable to come unless he is carried. So the friends’ faith is worth marking: they could not cure him, but they could bring him, and Christ honoured the bringing. Intercession is the ministry of the four who tore up the roof. And the word that met the man was sovereign and free — Son, thy sins be forgiven thee — spoken before he asked it, spoken by the One who has power on earth to forgive. When such a word comes, the paralysis of the will breaks, and the man who could not stir rises, takes up his bed, and walks home glorifying God.
roots_summary: The word is paralysis worn down by English use — the body loosed from the will’s command.
roots_lines: Palsy — a contraction of paralysis, Old French paralisie, Greek paralusis.
The Greek means “a loosing aside” — the limbs unstrung from the will.
The palsied man cannot come; he must be brought (Mar 2:3).
Christ pardoned first and healed second, on purpose (Mar 2:5; Mat 9:6).
The cure was the public receipt of the Son of man’s authority to forgive.
usage: Sick of the palsy: the man who cannot rise until Another commands him.
Son, thy sins be forgiven thee — the pardon came before the bed was ever lifted.
Christ healed the palsy that men might know He had power on earth to forgive sins.

etymology: From the Latin lunaticus, “moon-struck,” from luna, “the moon” — the old popular notion being that the falling sickness waxed and waned with the moon. The Authorized Version keeps the received English word of 1611; the Greek is seleniazomai, formed the same way.
biblical_def: Lunatick is the Authorized Version’s word for the falling sickness — the affliction that seizes a man and throws him down in convulsions. The English name and the Greek name behind it both carry an old folk-notion, that the fits followed the moon; the word is a description of what men observed, not a doctrine of what caused it. Scripture itself is careful. Matthew lists the sufferers side by side and does not confuse them: “those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them” (Mat 4:24). Devils are one class; lunaticks another; palsied men a third. The Word of God does not say that every convulsion is a devil, nor that no convulsion ever is. In one grievous case it was: a father knelt and cried, “Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water” (Mat 17:15), and the cure was an exorcism — “And Jesus rebuked the devil; and he departed out of him: and the child was cured from that very hour” (Mat 17:18). Mark records the same deliverance with the LORD charging a dumb and deaf spirit to come out and enter no more (Mar 9:25). The doctrine is not moon-lore but dominion: disease obeys Christ, and devils obey Him, and the ruined body and the invaded soul are alike restored at His word.
webster_summary: One affected with the falling sickness; in the old usage, one whose fits were thought to follow the changes of the moon.
webster_full: LUNATICK, affected with the disorder anciently supposed to be influenced by the moon; subject to the falling sickness or to fits of derangement.
From Latin lunaticus, from luna, the moon — a name drawn from an old popular observation, not from a cause.
The Greek seleniazomai (Mat 4:24; 17:15) is formed on selene, the moon, in exactly the same way.
Scripture lists the lunatick apart from the demoniac and the palsied (Mat 4:24).
In Mat 17:15 the affliction was demonic, and Christ cast the devil out.
scriptures: Mat 4:24

And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water.
And Jesus rebuked the devil; and he departed out of him: and the child was cured from that very hour.
Mar 9:25
When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him.
corruption_summary: An old descriptive word now used as an insult; and a modern age that denies devils altogether, having explained the invisible world away.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet on this word. The first is common cruelty: lunatic has passed out of medicine and into the mouth as a term of contempt, flung at the enemy in an argument. Scripture never uses it so. In the Gospels the lunatick is a son whose father falls at Christ’s feet, an afflicted body carried to mercy; and the church that mocks such a sufferer has forgotten both the compassion of her Lord and the fragility of her own frame. Afflicted image-bearers are to be pitied, borne with, and brought to Christ — never made a jest. The second corruption is the modern materialism that hears Matthew 17 and hurries to assure us that the boy simply had a disease and the first century did not know better. That is unbelief dressed as learning. The evangelist knew the difference; he named devils, lunaticks, and palsied men in one breath as three things, and then reported that this particular affliction was demonic and departed at a rebuke.

Hold both halves and you will hold the truth. Sickness is real, and it is sickness — the body groaning under the curse that came in with Adam, not proof of any special guilt in the sufferer. Devils are real, and they are devils — not a metaphor for what an unenlightened age could not diagnose. Christ’s authority covers the whole field: He healed all manner of disease throughout Syria, and He cast out the spirit that had thrown a boy into the fire and the water since childhood. Neither the physician nor the exorcist is our hope; the LORD Jesus is. And in an age that will not name the devil and an age that once saw him behind every fever, the sober middle is simply the text: bring the afflicted to Christ, ask mercy as that father did, and leave the diagnosis with the One who commands both flesh and fiends.
roots_summary: The word means “moon-struck,” the old name for the falling sickness — a description, not a cause.
roots_lines: Lunatick — Latin lunaticus, from luna, “the moon.”
The Greek seleniazomai is built the same way, on selene, the moon.
Both names record an old observation of recurring fits, not a doctrine of causes.
Mat 4:24 lists lunaticks apart from the demon-possessed and the palsied.
In Mat 17:15–18 the affliction was demonic and left at Christ’s rebuke.
usage: The lunatick of the Gospels is an afflicted sufferer carried to Christ, never a figure of fun.
Matthew names devils, lunaticks, and palsied men as three things, not one.
Christ’s dominion reaches disease and devils alike — and the boy was cured that very hour.

etymology: A worn form of the Middle English ydropesie, from the Greek hudrops, “watery,” from hudor, “water”; the disease in which water gathers in the body, swelling the limbs and belly with a thirst no drinking can quench.
biblical_def: The dropsy is the water-sickness — a body swollen and waterlogged, heavy, and tormented by a thirst that drinking only worsens. Luke the physician alone records the case, and he sets it in a room full of watching enemies: “And it came to pass, as he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the sabbath day, that they watched him. And, behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy” (Luk 14:1–2). The man stood there like a trap set and baited. Christ did not evade it; He sprang it first: “And Jesus answering spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?” (Luk 14:3). They held their peace, for the question had no answer that would not condemn them. “And he took him, and healed him, and let him go” (Luk 14:4). Then He turned their own practice upon their consciences: “Which of you shall have an ass or an ox fallen into a pit, and will not straightway pull him out on the sabbath day?” (Luk 14:5). They would haul a beast out of a hole on the LORD’s day and grudge a man his health. The sabbath was made for man, and the Lord of the sabbath keeps it best who heals on it. The dropsical man asked nothing, said nothing, and went home whole.
webster_summary: A morbid collection of water in the body or its parts; the swelling, water-sickness with its unquenchable thirst.
webster_full: DROPSY, an unnatural collection of water in any part of the body, attended with swelling and with a thirst not relieved by drinking.
From Middle English ydropesie, Greek hudrops, “watery,” from hudor, water.
It is the disease of a man full of water and dying of thirst — a parable in flesh.
Luke, the beloved physician, alone names it (Luk 14:2).
Christ healed it on the sabbath before lawyers and Pharisees who had set the case as a snare.
scriptures: Luk 14:2
And, behold, there was a certain man before him which had the dropsy.
Luk 14:3
And Jesus answering spake unto the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?
Luk 14:4
And they held their peace. And he took him, and healed him, and let him go;
Luk 14:1
And it came to pass, as he went into the house of one of the chief Pharisees to eat bread on the sabbath day, that they watched him.
corruption_summary: A one-verse disease that exposes two errors about the LORD’s day — the legalism that forbids mercy on it, and the laxity that forbids nothing at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The Pharisees’ error was to make the fourth commandment a fence against mercy. They had multiplied rules until a swollen man could not be healed and a hungry disciple could not rub an ear of corn, and they sat watching the Son of God to see whether He would do good, that they might accuse Him for it. That spirit is not extinct. Wherever the LORD’s day is kept as a performance of scruples rather than a delight in God, and wherever a congregation is more scandalised by a broken custom than by a neighbour left in his misery, the lawyers of Luke 14 are still at table. Christ’s question is the permanent rebuke: Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day? They held their peace, because the law they claimed to guard was on His side and not on theirs.

But the opposite error is the one our own age commits, and it is worse. Having heard that Christ healed on the sabbath, the modern professor concludes that the day means nothing — that the Christian sabbath is a Jewish relic, and the LORD’s day a slot in the schedule to be filled with commerce, sport, and errands, church attended when convenient. That is not liberty; it is the loss of a creation ordinance and a covenant gift. The 1689 Confession holds the Christian sabbath as a positive, moral, perpetual commandment, changed to the first day of the week in memory of Christ’s resurrection, kept by a holy resting from worldly employments and recreations, and taken up with worship and with the duties of necessity and mercy. The dropsical man is precisely the duty of mercy. Christ did not abolish the day; He cleared it of Pharisees and filled it with healing.
roots_summary: The word means “watery” — the body swollen with water and burning with thirst.
roots_lines: Dropsy — Middle English ydropesie, from Greek hudrops, “watery.”
Root hudor, “water” — the same root behind our hydrant and hydraulic.
The sufferer is full of water and thirsty still — drinking increases the disease.
A KJV hapax, recorded only by Luke the physician (Luk 14:2).
Its healing is the fourth of Luke’s sabbath-day miracles and the sharpest.
usage: The dropsy: full of water, and thirsty still — the very picture of the sinner in his pleasures.
Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day? — and they held their peace.
He took him, and healed him, and let him go: no debate, no apology, no delay.

etymology: Withered, from the Old English widrian, to dry up or shrivel (a doublet of weather); with hand, Old English hand. The Greek xeros means simply “dry” — a hand dried up, shrunken, and dead to use.
biblical_def: The withered hand is a dried and shrunken hand, useless to its owner. Luke, with a physician’s eye, notes which one: “there was a man whose right hand was withered” (Luk 6:6) — the working hand, the trade gone with it. Christ met him in the synagogue on the sabbath, and the watchers were already in their places: “And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him” (Mar 3:2). He would not heal in a corner. He said, Stand forth, and set the man in the midst where every eye must see, and asked whether it were lawful to do good or evil on the sabbath days, to save life or to destroy it. Then came the command that cannot be obeyed: “Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other” (Mar 3:5). This is the gospel in one gesture. Christ commands the very thing the man has no power to do, and the power comes in the commanding; grace supplies what the law requires. So the dead in trespasses are told to repent and believe, and the effectual call creates the obedience it demands. Mark the two hardnesses side by side: a hand withered, and hearts withered worse — for the LORD looked round in anger, grieved for their hardness, and they went out and “took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him” (Mar 3:6). On a day of mercy they plotted a murder.
webster_summary: A hand dried up and shrunken, dead to use; healed by Christ in the synagogue on the sabbath at the word, Stretch forth thine hand.
webster_full: WITHERED, dried; shrunk; shriveled; wanting the natural moisture and strength of life.
From Old English widrian, to dry up — kin to weather, which wastes what it beats upon.
The Greek xeros, “dry,” describes a limb shrunken past use.
Luke notes it was the right hand (Luk 6:6) — the man’s livelihood.
Christ commanded what the man could not do, and the doing came with the command (Mar 3:5).
scriptures: Mar 3:1
And he entered again into the synagogue; and there was a man there which had a withered hand.
Mar 3:5

And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
Luk 6:10
And looking round about upon them all, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thy hand. And he did so: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
Mar 3:6
And the Pharisees went forth, and straightway took counsel with the Herodians against him, how they might destroy him.
corruption_summary: A miracle constantly turned into its opposite — made a proof that the sinner has power in himself, when it is the classic proof that he has none.
corruption_paragraphs: The synergist reads Stretch forth thine hand and hears a demand addressed to a native ability: the man had to do his part, and God did the rest. But the man had no part to do. The hand was dry; that is the whole point of the story. He could no more stretch it out at the beginning of the verse than at the beginning of the day; what changed was not his willingness but Christ’s word, which carried its own power into a dead limb and made the stretching possible in the act of commanding it. So Augustine prayed that God would give what He commands and command what He will, and so the Reformed have always read the imperatives of the gospel. God bids Lazarus come forth and the dead man comes; God bids the sinner believe and the believing is itself the gift (Eph 2:8–9). To read the withered hand as a hidden compliment to human free will is to make the one man in the synagogue who could not help himself into the hero of his own cure.

The second corruption is the Pharisees’, and it is the more dangerous because it wears a Bible. They kept the sabbath so strictly they could not bear a mercy on it, and their zeal for the letter had dried their hearts as thoroughly as that man’s hand was dried. Christ looked on them with anger — a holy anger the sentimental Jesus of modern preaching is never permitted — and was grieved for their hardness. Then they went straight out and made common cause with the Herodians, whom they despised, to murder the Healer. That is what religion without regeneration comes to: it will forgive a plot against Christ sooner than a good deed done on the wrong day. Ask which hand in that synagogue was the more withered, and the text has already answered.
roots_summary: A dried, shrunken hand — healed by a command the man had no strength to obey.
roots_lines: Withered — Old English widrian, to dry up, shrivel; a doublet of weather.
Greek xeros, “dry” — the limb wasted past use.
Luke the physician specifies the right hand (Luk 6:6).
Stretch forth thine hand — grace giving what the command requires (Mar 3:5).
The hardness of the watching hearts is the true withering of the chapter (Mar 3:5–6).
usage: A withered hand is a dried hand — not weak, but dead to use.
Stretch forth thine hand: the command creates the obedience it demands.
His hand was restored whole as the other — and the Pharisees went out to plot a murder.

etymology: From the Old French mahaignier, “to wound, to mutilate, to cripple,” whence also the noun mayhem; hence deprived of a limb or of the use of one, mutilated, crippled.
biblical_def: To be maimed is to be mutilated — a limb lost or ruined, the body permanently broken. The word runs through the Gospels in three directions, and each is worth having. First, the maimed are healed: “great multitudes came unto him, having with them those that were lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and he healed them” (Mat 15:30), so that the crowd marvelled “when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole” (Mat 15:31). Christ restores what sin and a cursed world have torn away. Second, the maimed man is set up as the wise man in the fiercest saying about mortification: “if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched” (Mar 9:43; cf. Mat 18:8). The LORD is not commanding self-mutilation; He is measuring hell. If it were literally a choice between a hand and heaven, the hand should go without argument — therefore deal with the beloved sin as ruthlessly as that. Third, the maimed are the guests: “when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (Luk 14:13), and when the invited excused themselves the master sent to the streets and lanes for “the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind” (Luk 14:21). The banquet fills with cripples. That is the gospel: the maimed come in, and at the last are made whole.
webster_summary: Deprived of a limb or of its use; mutilated, crippled, permanently disabled in the body.
webster_full: MAIMED, crippled; disabled in a limb; deprived of a necessary part of the body.
From Old French mahaignier, to wound or mutilate — the same root as mayhem.
Christ healed the maimed in multitudes and made them whole (Mat 15:30–31).
Better to enter into life maimed than to go whole into hell (Mar 9:43).
The gospel feast is filled with the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind (Luk 14:21).
scriptures: And great multitudes came unto him, having with them those that were lame, blind, dumb, maimed, and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and he healed them:
Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel.
Mar 9:43
And if thy hand offend thee, cut it off: it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched:
But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind:
corruption_summary: The mortification texts blunted into metaphor by an age that will not believe in hell, and the feast texts emptied of the repentance that fills them.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 9:43 is among the most softened verses in modern preaching. The reasoning runs that Christ was using hyperbole, and hyperbole may be discounted, and so the saying is reduced to a mild counsel about balance and boundaries. But the figure is hyperbolic only in the surgery; the arithmetic is literal. Christ names the alternative in plain words — hell, and the fire that never shall be quenched — and it is that unquenchable fire which makes the amputation reasonable. Take the everlasting fire away and the verse is madness; leave it in and the verse is common sense. Mortification, then, is not the pruning of excess but the killing of sin: Paul’s mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth (Col 3:5), his if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live (Rom 8:13). Owen said it plainly — be killing sin or it will be killing you.

The feast texts suffer the opposite corruption. Luke 14 is quoted to underwrite a gospel of mere welcome: the master calls the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind, therefore Christ receives everyone as they are and requires nothing. But look at the same chapter’s close, where the LORD tells the multitudes that whosoever will not bear his cross and come after Him cannot be His disciple, and bids them count the cost. The maimed are brought in freely, and they are brought in to a table where the Master is Lord. Grace does not consult our qualifications — the guests had none, which is why the invitation had to be free — but grace summons the guest to repentance and to a new obedience. The banquet is not a room where the crippled are congratulated on their crippling; it is the house of the God who at the last will make the maimed whole.
roots_summary: The word means mutilated or crippled — a body permanently deprived of a limb or its use.
roots_lines: Maimed — Old French mahaignier, “to wound, mutilate, cripple.”
The same root gives English mayhem, the old law-term for maiming a man.
Christ healed the maimed and the multitude glorified the God of Israel (Mat 15:31).
Better maimed in life than whole in hell — the measure of mortification (Mar 9:43).
The gospel feast is stocked with the maimed and the halt (Luk 14:13, 21).
usage: The maimed were cast down at Jesus’ feet, and He made them whole.
Better to enter into life maimed: Christ measures the sin against the fire.
Call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind — the guest list of grace.

etymology: From hoar, Old English har, “grey, white with age” (as in the hoary head of Pro 16:31), with frost; hence the white rime that whitens the ground in the night as age whitens a head.
biblical_def: Hoarfrost is the white rime that settles on the ground in a cold night, greying the field as age greys a head. Scripture uses it twice to great purpose. First, it is the measure of the manna. When the dew was gone up, “behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground” (Exo 16:14) — bread from heaven, lying in the morning as commonly as frost, gathered daily, sufficient and never storable, so that Israel learned to live by the hand of God from one dawn to the next. Christ took up that manna and said, I am the bread of life. Second, the hoarfrost is a witness to the LORD’s effortless government of the elements: “He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes. He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?” (Psa 147:16–17). The Psalmist does not describe weather; he describes a Sovereign scattering frost as a man scatters ashes from a hearth, and asks who can stand before His cold. Then in one line the same word that binds the frost releases it: “He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow” (Psa 147:18). The God whose word freezes and whose word thaws is the God whose word saves; and the next verse of that psalm turns immediately to His statutes given to Jacob. Frost and Scripture come from the same mouth.
webster_summary: The white rime or frozen dew that whitens the ground on a cold morning — frost the colour of a hoary head.
webster_full: HOARFROST, the white particles of frozen dew; rime; the frost that whitens the ground in a cold night.
From hoar, Old English har, “grey or white with age” — compare the hoary head of Pro 16:31.
The manna lay in the wilderness as small as the hoar frost on the ground (Exo 16:14).
The LORD scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes and casteth forth His ice like morsels (Psa 147:16–17).
He sendeth out His word and melteth them — the same word that binds and looses the elements (Psa 147:18).
scriptures: And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
He giveth snow like wool: he scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.
He casteth forth his ice like morsels: who can stand before his cold?
He sendeth out his word, and melteth them: he causeth his wind to blow, and the waters flow.
corruption_summary: A small white word for a great doctrine — that the weather is governed, not merely observed; and a modern instinct that has emptied the sky of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption here is not a redefinition of the word but the quiet deism of the modern mind, which grants that God made the world and denies that He runs it. Frost, on that view, is a mechanism: pressure, dew point, radiative cooling — a closed system of causes with no hand in it. Scripture describes the identical frost and never once treats the mechanism as a rival to the Maker. He giveth snow; He scattereth the hoarfrost; He casteth forth His ice; and the question who can stand before his cold? is not rhetoric but reverence. The mechanism is the manner of His working, not a substitute for it. A church that has absorbed the deist reflex will pray about the soul and never about the harvest, will thank God for grace and not for rain, and will find the doctrine of providence a lovely abstraction it does not actually believe on a cold morning.

Recover the doctrine that Providence is particular. The LORD upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and all things, from the greatest to the least, by His most wise and holy providence — and the frost on the grass is one of the least, deliberately chosen by the Psalmist for that reason. Two comforts follow. First, the God who scatters frost like ashes provides bread like frost: Israel woke to manna lying as thick and as common as rime, and learned that daily bread comes from a daily hand. Second, the word that governs the elements is the word that governs the soul. He sendeth out His word and melteth them — and the same psalm goes on at once to say that He sheweth His word unto Jacob, His statutes and His judgments unto Israel. The voice that thaws the frozen ground is the voice that thaws a frozen heart, and neither is beyond it.
roots_summary: The word joins hoar, “grey with age,” to frost — the white rime on a cold ground.
roots_lines: Hoarfrost — hoar (Old English har, “grey, white”) + frost.
The same hoar gives the hoary head, the crown of glory of Pro 16:31.
The manna was as small as the hoar frost on the ground (Exo 16:14).
God scatters it like ashes from a hearth (Psa 147:16) — effortless sovereignty.
His word binds the frost and His word melts it (Psa 147:17–18).
usage: As small as the hoar frost on the ground — the measure of the manna.
He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes: the weather is governed, not merely observed.
Who can stand before his cold? — and yet He sendeth out His word, and melteth them.

etymology: From whirl (Middle English whirlen, of Norse origin, to turn rapidly) and wind; the Hebrew ce'arah and suphah alike name the tempest that turns and sweeps, the storm-wind of God’s coming.
biblical_def: A whirlwind is a turning tempest — the storm-wind that sweeps up and carries off whatever it finds. In Scripture it is God’s chariot, God’s pulpit, and God’s harvest-sickle. It is His chariot when Elijah is taken: “there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” (2Ki 2:11) — the LORD had told Elisha beforehand that He would take up His prophet so (2Ki 2:1). It is His pulpit when Job’s long argument is answered: the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind, and the answer was not an explanation but a catechism about wild goats and cloud and snow, until the man who had demanded a hearing laid his hand upon his mouth. God speaks from the storm, not around it. And it is His sickle in the prophets: “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hos 8:7) — the classic statement that sin’s harvest exceeds its seed, that a nation which plants emptiness reaps ruin, and that the yield of idolatry has no stalk and no meal. Nahum sets the whole doctrine in one verse: “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nah 1:3). The tempest that terrifies the wicked is only the dust kicked up by the walking of God.
webster_summary: A violent turning wind; a tempest that whirls and sweeps — in Scripture the chariot, the pulpit, and the judgment of God.
webster_full: WHIRLWIND, a violent wind moving in a circle or spiral; a tempest that sweeps and carries off.
From whirl, to turn rapidly, and wind; Hebrew ce'arah, suphah, the storm-wind.
Elijah was carried up by a whirlwind into heaven (2Ki 2:11).
The LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38:1) — He speaks from the storm.
They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind: sin’s harvest exceeds its seed (Hos 8:7).
scriptures: And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
And it came to pass, when the LORD would take up Elijah into heaven by a whirlwind, that Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
Hos 8:7
For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up.
Nah 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
corruption_summary: A storm-word flattened into a figure of speech, and a Book of Job read as a poem about the problem of pain rather than a theophany.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has thinned in modern mouths to a metaphor for a busy week, and the doctrine has thinned with it. Behind the flattening lies a settled unwillingness to grant that God governs storms — that Nahum meant what he said when he put the LORD’s way in the whirlwind and made the thunderheads the dust of His feet. So the whirlwind of Job 38 is treated as a literary device, and the book is preached as an inquiry into the problem of suffering that ends, disappointingly, without an answer. But Job did not receive an argument because he did not need one; he needed God, and God came — personally, audibly, out of the tempest — and asked him where he was when the foundations were laid. The book ends with a man silenced and satisfied. That is the answer, and only a generation that thinks God owes it explanations could miss it.

The second flattening is Hosea 8:7 reduced to a proverb about consequences. It is more than that: it is covenant judgment. Israel had sown the wind — calf-worship at Bethel, treaties with Assyria, kings set up without the LORD — and the whirlwind that came was not an impersonal blowback but the hand of a God who will not at all acquit the wicked. The harvest law stands for nations still, and for men: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Gal 6:7), and the reaping is always larger than the sowing. Yet the same whirlwind that carries away the chaff carried Elijah home. To the wicked the storm is judgment; to the LORD’s servant it is a chariot. The difference is not in the weather but in whose you are.
roots_summary: A turning tempest — in Scripture the chariot, the pulpit, and the judgment-harvest of God.
roots_lines: Whirlwind — whirl (to turn rapidly) + wind; Hebrew ce'arah, suphah.
It is God’s chariot: Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven (2Ki 2:11).
It is God’s pulpit: the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38:1).
It is God’s sickle: they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind (Hos 8:7).
Nah 1:3 — the clouds are the dust of His feet; the storm is His walking.
usage: Elijah went up by a whirlwind: to the servant of God the storm is a chariot.
They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind — the harvest exceeds the seed.
The LORD hath His way in the whirlwind: He is never merely in the calm.

etymology: From the Middle English brinston, “burning stone” (Old English bryne, a burning, + stan, stone) — sulphur, which takes fire readily and burns with a choking blue flame and a stench.
biblical_def: Brimstone is the burning stone — sulphur, which kindles at a touch, burns with a livid flame and a suffocating reek, and leaves the ground it has fallen on barren. Scripture reserves it almost wholly for judgment, and the pattern begins at Sodom: “Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven” (Gen 19:24). That was no natural disaster overtaking a city; it was rain, sent, by name, from the LORD out of heaven, upon cities whose sin was very grievous. The Psalmist makes it the portion of every wicked man: “Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: this shall be the portion of their cup” (Psa 11:6). Christ Himself takes up Sodom’s overthrow and sets it as the very type of the day of His revealing: “But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all” (Luk 17:29) — even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed. And the Revelation carries the word to its final use: the beast, the false prophet, and the devil are cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where they shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever (Rev 20:10); and “the fearful, and unbelieving… and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death” (Rev 21:8). The word is a warning, and it is spoken by Christ oftener than by anyone.
webster_summary: Sulphur; the burning stone that kindles at a touch — in Scripture the settled emblem of divine judgment and of the lake of fire.
webster_full: BRIMSTONE, sulphur; a hard, brittle, inflammable substance which burns with a blue flame and a suffocating odour.
From Middle English brinston — Old English bryne, “a burning,” + stan, “stone.”
The LORD rained brimstone and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah out of heaven (Gen 19:24).
It is the portion of the cup of the wicked (Psa 11:6).
The lake which burneth with fire and brimstone is the second death (Rev 21:8).
scriptures: Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;
Psa 11:6
Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, and an horrible tempest: this shall be the portion of their cup.
But the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
corruption_summary: The plainest word in Scripture for eternal punishment, denied outright by universalism, extinguished by annihilationism, and mocked into silence by the sneer “fire and brimstone.”
corruption_paragraphs: Three corruptions attack this word, and all three end in the same place. Universalism holds that God will at last save every soul, that hell is a purge and not a portion, and that the lake of fire empties. Scripture does not permit it: the same adjective that measures the life of the righteous measures the punishment of the wicked (Mat 25:46), and the Revelation says the tormenting is day and night for ever and ever (Rev 20:10). Annihilationism grants the fire and denies the duration, teaching that the lost are consumed and cease to be. But a fire that never shall be quenched (Mar 9:43) and a smoke of torment that ascendeth up for ever (Rev 14:11) is not a fire that finishes its work in an hour. The third corruption is not an argument at all but a sneer: fire-and-brimstone preaching, used to shame any man who warns his hearers of what Christ warned His. It is worth remembering who preached this doctrine most. The gentlest lips that ever spoke are the lips that said everlasting fire.

There is no way to be kind about hell except to tell the truth about it. The LORD Jesus set Sodom’s burning before His disciples as the pattern of the day of His revealing, and He did it to save them from it. That is what the doctrine is for. Sodom is preached in the New Testament as an example (2Pe 2:6; Jud 7) — a city given over, warned, and consumed — and set alongside it stands Lot, dragged out by the hand while he lingered, saved not by his merit but by the mercy of God. That is every believer’s history. The brimstone fell the same day Lot went out; not before, not after. Judgment waited on the deliverance of the elect, and it always does. So the word is not a bludgeon but an alarm, and the man who hears it and flees to Christ will find that the fire which is the portion of the wicked’s cup was drunk to the dregs by Another in his stead.
roots_summary: The word means “burning stone” — sulphur, the settled emblem of God’s judgment.
roots_lines: Brimstone — Old English bryne (“a burning”) + stan (“stone”).
It names sulphur: quick to kindle, choking in its smoke, sterile where it falls.
Sodom’s overthrow is the pattern: brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven (Gen 19:24).
It is the portion of the cup of the wicked (Psa 11:6) — a measured, judicial draught.
Its last use is the lake of fire and brimstone, the second death (Rev 21:8).
usage: The LORD rained brimstone upon Sodom: judgment sent by name, from heaven.
Fire and brimstone is the portion of their cup — a measured, judicial portion.
The same day that Lot went out, it rained fire — judgment waits on the rescue of the elect.

etymology: From the Old English thistel, a prickly weed of the field; in Scripture the companion of the thorn, and with it the standing sign of the ground cursed for Adam’s sake.
biblical_def: The thistle is a prickly weed — useless, self-seeding, quick to hold ground, hard to root out. Its first appearance in Scripture fixes its meaning for ever, for it is part of the sentence passed in Eden: “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field” (Gen 3:18). The earth itself was cursed for man’s sake, and thistles are the visible proof of it. Every field that must be weeded preaches Genesis 3; the ground gives its increase now only against resistance, and man eats bread in the sweat of his face. From that root the word grows three ways. It is the emblem of pride in Jehoash’s stinging parable to Amaziah: “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle” (2Ki 14:9) — the weed proposed an alliance with the cedar and was trampled by a passing beast, and Amaziah, who would not hear it, was beaten. It is the emblem of a false profession in the LORD’s test of teachers: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Mat 7:16). And it is the emblem of desolation, springing up on the altars of a false worship (Hos 10:8). Nature is uniform: a thistle bears thistles, and a false heart bears its own fruit.
webster_summary: A prickly weed of the field; with the thorn, the sign of the ground cursed for man’s sake.
webster_full: THISTLE, a prickly plant of the fields, of many species, troublesome to the husbandman.
From Old English thistel; in Scripture always coupled with the thorn.
Thorns and thistles are the ground’s answer to Adam’s sin (Gen 3:18).
Jehoash likened proud Amaziah to a thistle courting a cedar (2Ki 14:9).
Men do not gather figs of thistles: the fruit declares the tree (Mat 7:16).
scriptures: Gen 3:18
Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;

And Jehoash the king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, Give thy daughter to my son to wife: and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon, and trode down the thistle.
Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended.
Hos 10:8

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.
corruption_summary: A weed whose testimony is denied — for if there was no historical fall, the thistle is simply nature, and the world is as God first made it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is not linguistic but doctrinal: the denial of a historical Adam and a real curse. Theistic evolution and its evangelical borrowers must read Genesis 3 as a parable of the human condition, which means the thorns and thistles were always there, that thistle and famine and death belong to the world as God pronounced it very good, and that the groaning of the creation Paul describes (Rom 8:20–22) is not a wound but a design. Scripture will not bend to it. The ground was cursed for thy sake, at a moment, because of a man’s sin; the thistle is an intruder in a good creation, not a feature of it. Deny that and you have made God the author of the curse rather than the Judge who pronounced it, and you have cut the nerve of the gospel, for the Last Adam undoes what the first Adam did, and if the first Adam did nothing there is nothing to undo.

Three lessons stand once the doctrine is held. First, labour is now against resistance, and the sweat of the face is part of the sentence — which is why every honest day’s work is a small preaching of Genesis 3 and a small groaning after redemption. Second, pride is a thistle: Jehoash’s parable is cruel and true, the weed proposing marriage to the cedar and trodden down by a beast that never noticed it, and Amaziah lost his kingdom refusing the lesson. Third, fruit is the test of profession — men do not gather figs of thistles, and no confession of orthodoxy, no warmth of manner, no crowd, can make a corrupt tree bear good fruit. Yet the curse has a limit and a term. The Man who wore the thorns of Adam’s curse upon His head bore the whole sentence, and in the day of His appearing the ground itself is delivered: instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier the myrtle tree (Isa 55:13).
roots_summary: A prickly field-weed; with the thorn, the standing sign of the curse on the ground.
roots_lines: Thistle — Old English thistel, a prickly weed of the fields.
First named in the sentence on the ground: thorns also and thistles (Gen 3:18).
It is the intruder in a good creation, not a part of its original design.
Jehoash’s parable makes it the emblem of pride overreaching (2Ki 14:9).
Christ makes it the test of teachers: no figs grow on thistles (Mat 7:16).
usage: Thorns also and thistles — every weeded field preaches Genesis 3.
The thistle courted the cedar and was trodden down: pride overreaching itself.
Do men gather figs of thistles? The fruit, not the profession, declares the tree.

etymology: From the Old English hind, the female of the red deer (the male being the hart); the Hebrew ayyalah, a doe — a creature proverbial for swiftness, sure footing on the heights, gentleness, and travail in bearing.
biblical_def: A hind is a doe, the female deer — swift, sure-footed on broken ground, gentle, and known for her hard travail in calving. Scripture takes each of these traits and makes doctrine of it. The chief use is the sure foot on the height: “He maketh my feet like hinds' feet, and setteth me upon my high places” (Psa 18:33; the same in David’s song at 2Sa 22:34). The deer does not climb the crag by care but by a made nature; God gives the footing, and the man He equips stands where he could never have stood. Habakkuk takes that line and sets it at the end of the darkest chapter in the Minor Prophets, after the fig tree fails, the vine bears nothing, the flock is cut off and the stall is empty: “The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places” (Hab 3:19). That is joy in the LORD with the barn empty — the highest note faith reaches this side of glory. Jacob blesses Naphtali as “a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words” (Gen 49:21), the freed doe running with good tidings. Solomon commends the wife of youth as “the loving hind and pleasant roe” (Pro 5:19), setting covenant delight against the strange woman. And in the storm-psalm the LORD’s voice reaches even the hidden birth: “The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve” (Psa 29:9).
webster_summary: The female of the red deer; a doe — proverbial for swiftness, sure footing on the heights, and gentleness.
webster_full: HIND, the female of the red deer or stag; a doe.
From Old English hind; the male is the hart. Hebrew ayyalah.
Hinds' feet are the emblem of sure footing on dangerous heights (Psa 18:33; 2Sa 22:34).
Habakkuk claims them when every crop and flock has failed (Hab 3:19).
Naphtali is blessed as a hind let loose, giving goodly words (Gen 49:21).
scriptures: He maketh my feet like hinds' feet, and setteth me upon my high places.
Hab 3:19
The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words.
Psa 29:9
The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory.
corruption_summary: A promise of sure footing routinely misquoted as a promise of easy ground — and Habakkuk’s joy severed from the famine that gives it its meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: Hinds' feet on high places has become a favourite line of devotional sentiment, and in the borrowing it has been turned inside out. The popular sense is that God will lift the believer above his troubles into a serene upland where the difficulty is gone. But the high places of Psalm 18 are battlefields and crags — David is describing a warrior set on ground he must hold — and the gift is not a smoother path but a changed foot. Grace does not flatten the mountain; it makes the climber fit for it. The same misreading strips Habakkuk 3:19 from its verse before. Take the fig tree, the vine, the olive, the field, the flock, and the stall away, and only then quote the promise, and you will hear what the prophet meant: yet I will rejoice in the LORD with nothing left in the barn. Rejoicing when the harvest is in requires no faith at all.

Two things follow for the believer. The first is the doctrine of perseverance rightly stated: the saint keeps his footing because he is kept, not because he is careful. He maketh my feet like hinds' feet; he setteth me upon my high places — the verbs are all His. That is why the Confession can say the saints shall certainly persevere, not on the strength of their own free will, but on the immutability of the decree, the merit and intercession of Christ, and the abiding of the Spirit. The second is that the LORD’s care descends to the hidden and the small. The voice that shakes the wilderness and breaks the cedars is the same voice that brings a doe safely through her travail in a forest no man is watching. A God attentive enough to time the calving of a hind is attentive enough to time your deliverance, and the feet He makes will carry you over the ground He has appointed.
roots_summary: The doe of the red deer — swift, sure-footed on the heights, gentle, and hard in travail.
roots_lines: Hind — Old English hind, the female red deer; the male is the hart.
Hebrew ayyalah, a doe — proverbial for swiftness and sure footing.
Hinds' feet = a made ability to stand on broken, dangerous ground (Psa 18:33).
Habakkuk claims the promise with the fig tree failing and the stall empty (Hab 3:19).
Naphtali, a hind let loose, runs bearing goodly words (Gen 49:21).
usage: He maketh my feet like hinds’ feet: not an easier path, but a surer foot.
Habakkuk sings of hinds’ feet with the barn empty — that is faith at its height.
Naphtali, a hind let loose, giving goodly words: freedom in the service of good tidings.
